title: Carey's ritzy Red Garter club fails; Carey as an amateur bassist
summary: Carey's Red Garter flopped because he drove away neighbourhood customers with dress rules, and he loved playing though not a musician, even imitating Johnny Ray.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: When he got his own club, what was that? Do you remember the name?
Well he called that Red Garter, I think
it was.
Red Garter.
And -- that's a pretty good ways out, and we used to work there, but then it didn't turn out so good.
Why?

Because -- well, I don't know. He has an idea I think back in his mind he wanted to -- he wanted to have a ritzy -- a ritzy place. I don't know. He didn't want the guys to come in there without a tie on, or in a jacket. He didn't want to serve them, you know, and it's a neighborhood where there were bars on the corner, you know. And -- I think he was his own worst enemy. I mean he chased the people away, and the business didn't show, and somebody else took over and rightaway the next -- the following week, man they started packing the joint, because the --

You know, a guy come in there, if a man has money, if he comes out and orders a lot of stuff and can't pay for it, aw, they throw him out. But regardless of what he's wearing, I would say, and if he's not disturbing the peace, or breaking up the joint, to heck with him! He's paying.
When this other fellow took over, these other people took over, did you play there then too, or only when -- only with Frank Carey.
No, I heard about it, you know.
: You heard about it. I see.
I heard about it later, and I wished I had of been, because the job was paying nice, but I don't know, Frank just --
: Was this about the same time that you were playing at the Embers?
Uh, yes.
: About that period?

Yes. Yes. I had played the Embers after that. I'm sure it had to be, because if I hadn't I know Frank would have said Herman, gee, I give you work. You're working regular. You go in there but you don't call me. Why don't you come -- I can hear him now.
(Laughter.)
See, that's just what he would have said. So that -- we --
: Was -- as a bass player, was he any good?
Naw, okay?
No? Okay,
(Laughter.)
: I see. That's why he stayed in Brooklyn.
Yeah, he owned a bass, and no, no he wasn't a musician. He knew it, and everybody that knew him

knew it. But he just loved to play. He told -- zooma, zooma, zooma, zooma, zooma, zooma -- you know? And he said what key is it? What key is it? I -- do I do so and so? I'd say E flat, I think, or G, or whatever it was. Okay, and we hit it off, and he say he wanted to do -- uh, Ray -- where he pull off the coat, left your hat on, and cry, and everything?
Oh, Johnny Ray.
Yeah! Oh he was -- and he'd go into this thing and chase everybody out of the place with his coat off, and that business, you know.
(Laughter.)
(Unintelligible) his own best friends, you know. They'd say oh, what the heck. I wouldn't -- I couldn't say anything. I didn't dare. I worked for the guy.
